definition: A structure that divides and provides the price roles and ranges of products, such as entry, core, and premium.
example: The core tier is empty in the jacket price-tier structure, so supplement the products.

definition: The degree to which a product's style, price, and wearing occasion match the target customer's taste and lifestyle.
example: The design is good, but check whether the length suits the target fit of commuting customers.
note: It refers to the suitability between customer and product. Distinguish it from fit, which means the actual measurements and silhouette when worn.

definition: The degree to which the expression of products, styling, and collaborations suits the brand's identity and product direction.
example: Even for a trending detail, review whether it fits our collection's brand fit.

definition: The appropriate time to sell a given product considering season, events, demand changes, and so on.
example: If delivery is late, you may miss the optimal sales timing for winter outerwear.

definition: The quantity first ordered or input when starting the sale or production of a new product.
example: Keep the initial order quantity small and reorder after seeing initial sales.
note: It concerns the first production or order quantity. Distinguish it from the sample-making quantity or the total seasonal order quantity.

definition: A plan deciding when and through which channel, price, and promotion to sell remaining products.
example: For end-of-season inventory, look at the sell-through plan by channel, not just the discount rate.

definition: A situation of being later than the agreed date for raw and sub-material supply, production, or delivery.
example: Check the impact of the sub-material delivery delay on the finished-goods arrival date.

definition: A session where a sample is worn to examine measurements, balance, movement, and so on, and decide pattern and sewing revisions.
example: In the fitting meeting, check whether the waist and rise are uncomfortable when seated.

definition: A sample remade to reflect the comments from the previous review.
example: In the revised sample, check whether the sleeve-width change and collar lifting are resolved.

definition: The size used as the reference when developing the pattern, measurements, and fit, and grading to other sizes.
example: Match the fit of the base size first, then review the size set.

definition: The ease added to body measurements in a garment for movement and silhouette.
example: Since the shirt has no stretch, check the wearing ease at the back and arms.

definition: A state in which the front-back and left-right length and position relationships achieve the intended balance when worn.
example: Examine the cause of the side seam rotating forward together with the front-back balance.
note: This is the context of a garment's pattern, measurements, and wearing balance. Distinguish it from design balance, which means visual weight on screen.

definition: Releasing products divided into set groups and timings within a season, or such a group.
example: Compose the second drop with lightweight outerwear to sell before the rainy season.
note: This is the context of sequential release in fashion. It differs from the general-business drop, which means excluding an agenda item or task.

definition: A style selected to represent the season's design direction or sales strategy.
example: Connect other outfits based on the silhouette of the key style.

definition: The work of lowering a product's cost by adjusting materials, sub-materials, processes, and so on.
example: Even when doing a cost down, zipper durability and sewing quality must be maintained.

definition: The cost standard to be met in product development, considering the selling price, profit, and distribution conditions.
example: It exceeds the target cost, so review alternatives for the fabric and sewing process.

definition: The work of breaking down costs by item such as fabric, sub-materials, labor, and processing to examine the cost structure.
example: In the cost analysis, check how much the embroidery labor accounts for.

definition: Deciding the fabric to use in production after reviewing quality, color, price, supply, and so on.
example: Before confirming the fabric, also check the shrinkage rate and delivery.

definition: A material reviewed in place of the existing fabric for reasons such as quality, price, or delivery.
example: For the alternative fabric, do not just look at color; also compare drape and post-wash measurements.

definition: A meeting before mass production where the relevant people align on specifications, approved samples, processes, quality standards, and schedule.
example: In the pre-production meeting, eliminate the differences between the approved sample and the work order.
note: This is a pre-mass-production meeting for garments. It differs in participants and review subject from the PPM held before a fashion editorial shoot.

definition: A procedure that approves starting mass production based on the reviewed sample and specifications.
example: After checking the revised sewing specifications, grant mass-production approval.

definition: A state of postponing the approval decision because there are unresolved matters in the sample or raw and sub-materials.
example: The lot-to-lot shade check is not finished, so that fabric is on approval hold.
note: It is a state before the review is finished. It does not necessarily mean final rejection or production cancellation.

definition: A standard for how and within what tolerance to inspect the measurements, sewing, and appearance of finished products.
example: Review the defect samples together so the brand and factory use the same inspection standard.

definition: A review process where the design's goals and intent are shared and colleagues find directions for improvement through questions and feedback.
example: In the critique, start with whether users can find information rather than whether it looks good.
note: It means a review for improvement, separate from a formal approval procedure. The method and participants differ by organization.

definition: The central idea and expressive direction for coherently developing goals and messages into form, color, typeface, composition, and so on.
example: Check whether the concept of approachable expertise shows through in the typeface and photos too.

definition: The visual character the design should pursue and the direction of choices that realize it.
example: Align the design direction around warm colors and clean forms.

definition: Different drafts presented separately for comparison and selection. Also agree on the scope of whether it is a simple color change or a fundamentally different concept.
example: Option A emphasizes information delivery, and Option B emphasizes brand impression.

definition: The central draft among several to be proposed or developed first.
example: Keep the structure of the main option while adjusting the title contrast more.

definition: A separate design draft prepared to respond to constraints of the existing draft or other possibilities.
example: Prepare a graphics-focused alternative draft in case using photos is difficult.

definition: The order in which the gaze moves according to the placement, size, contrast, and so on of elements on a screen or page.
example: To make people see the button after the title, check where to connect the visual flow.

definition: The degree to which the composition of characters and text allows content to be read and understood comfortably.
example: Adjust the body width and line spacing to improve the readability of long explanations.
note: It is explained as distinct from legibility, but in practice both are often called readability broadly. Specify what reading problem exists.

definition: The degree to which the forms of individual characters or symbols can be distinguished and recognized.
example: Compare the legibility of the numeral 1 and the letter I at small sizes.

definition: The degree to which the presence and position of a visual element stand out under conditions such as distance, light, and background.
example: Check whether the signage has sufficient visibility even from the end of the hallway.

definition: The amount and concentration of information contained within a given screen or page.
example: Reduce the information density of the first screen and split the detailed explanation into the next section.

definition: The degree to which an element draws the eye or feels heavy due to size, color, position, texture, and so on.
example: The left photo has strong visual weight, so balance it with the title on the right.

definition: The balance that elements' visual weight and spatial arrangement achieve across the whole.
example: Before just reducing the logo size, look at the balance of the photo and the whitespace.
note: It is the balance of visual weight and arrangement. It is a different subject from a garment's front-back wearing balance.

definition: The characteristic and completeness with which relationships of form, proportion, line, and plane are visually composed.
example: Review whether the small protrusion of the symbol fits the overall formative quality.

definition: The property by which expressions, rules, and behaviors serving the same purpose are kept uniform across related screens and deliverables.
example: The same button's color differs by screen, so organize the design consistency.

definition: Subjective feedback that the placement, proportion, or connection does not fit well with surrounding elements or the intent.
example: Please point out specifically whether the awkward part is the photo ratio or the title position.
note: It is subjective feedback, not a precise process name. Explain the subject, reason, and desired result together to align the revision direction.

definition: Feedback describing a sense that the gaze and reading flow are blocked because elements are crowded or whitespace and separation are insufficient.
example: The card looks cramped, so try first increasing the whitespace between information groups.
note: Do not treat personal impressions as if they were numbers. Point out subjects to check together, such as information volume, whitespace, and font size.

definition: A working expression for adjusting size, contrast, weight, space, and so on so that important elements are seen first.
example: Add weight to the title, but do not make all the supporting text bold too.

definition: A working expression for refining elements' alignment, spacing, hierarchy, and style by a consistent standard.
example: Please tidy up the left baseline and the card spacing first.

definition: The size at which something is actually used or produced. Check it as distinct from a zoomed screen state.
example: Print the business card at actual size and check whether the text is legible.
note: For print, check against the actual output size; for screen, against the actual display environment.

definition: The area where important text and elements are placed, avoiding the effects of trimming, cropping, and screen edges.
example: Considering poster trimming tolerance, place the contact details within the safe area.
note: It is not the same area as bleed, the trimming margin. Keep important information inside the finished area.

definition: A decision that agrees on the information structure and main arrangement to serve as the basis for subsequent detailed work.
example: After the layout confirmation, proceed with photo retouching, but share any major structural changes separately.

definition: The work of checking whether the implemented or produced result matches the draft, rules, and intended behavior.
example: In design QA, compare long text and error states against the draft too.

definition: A revision unit in which one batch of feedback is collected, reflected, and reviewed again.
example: In this revision round, collect structural changes, and check typos next time.

definition: The work of organizing working source files such as layers, file names, links, and fonts so they can be handed over and revised.
example: Before delivery, use source file cleanup to check for missing images and unused layers.

definition: The process of reviewing the storyboard cuts in order to confirm directing intent, action, shooting, and production conditions.
example: In the storyboard reading, match the hand picking up the product with the direction of the next cut.

definition: The process where the cast and others read the script aloud to confirm dialogue, character relationships, and scene flow.
example: In the script reading, align the points where emotions shift and the pacing of the lines.

definition: A list organizing needed information such as the content, composition, and movement of the shots to be filmed.
example: Mark the essential hand insert and an alternative composition on the shot list.

definition: The work of dividing and organizing elements needed for production by scene, such as cast, location, props, costumes, and effects.
example: In the scene breakdown, check the spare costumes and equipment needed for the rain scene.

definition: The actual order of shooting, decided by considering location, cast, light, and setup separately from the story order.
example: Change the shooting order so the exterior cuts that need sunlight are shot first.

definition: The path along which cast, camera, or crew move within the scene and on the shooting location.
example: Check at rehearsal where the actors' movement path and the camera movement overlap.

definition: Deciding where and how the cast look, to create the scene's relationships and expression.
example: Even in a close-up without the other actor, match the eyeline to the same height.

definition: The mode of expression in acting shown through the intensity and character of lines, expressions, and gestures.
example: The situation is comic, but try keeping the acting tone serious.

definition: The flow in which a character's emotions change and continue along events and scenes.
example: Even if the shooting order changes, check that it can start from the emotional arc of the previous scene.

definition: The degree to which the connection of a character's actions and events is convincing within the work's setting and context.
example: The plausibility of suddenly leaving is weak, so add a clue in the earlier scene.

definition: A structure that stacks preceding scenes and information so that later events, emotions, and reactions feel convincing.
example: Build up with two cuts before the twist so the character's choice is understandable.
note: This is the context of stacking a video's scenes, emotions, and events. It differs in subject from the general-business usage of building up the grounds of a proposal.

definition: Pre-visualization that tests composition, blocking, and timing with simple video or 3D before the main shoot or final production.
example: Check the complex camera movement with previs and decide the set size.

definition: A rehearsal that checks the operation and transition timing of camera, lighting, sound, and equipment.
example: Before the cast enters, check the lighting transitions and recording status with a tech rehearsal.

definition: A rehearsal that runs a segment or program in order, as uninterrupted as possible, to check the flow and timing.
example: Once the individual setups are done, check the total runtime with a run-through.

definition: Alternatives for location, schedule, scenes, and so on to apply when weather changes make shooting difficult.
example: Write the indoor alternative cuts and the decision time for postponing the shoot into the weather plan.

definition: An editing method that first organizes the order and structure of content using text such as interview transcripts or scripts.
example: In the interview paper edit, select the key remarks, then move them to the timeline.

definition: An early edit that first strings selected scenes together to examine the overall content and structure.
example: In the assembly cut, check for missing explanations, then reduce the length afterward.
note: The standard for distinguishing it from a rough cut can differ by team. Check the review scope and completion level of the edit together.

definition: The point decided for which frame or action to cut on or connect.
example: Try moving the edit point to the frame where the hand begins to move.

definition: The progression speed and rhythm of the story as felt through cut lengths, information volume, and scene arrangement.
example: Adjust the pacing of the information-heavy middle to give the audience time to follow.

definition: A cut that repeats already-conveyed information or a similar scene.
example: Reduce redundant cuts where the feature explanation overlaps, and keep the actual-use scene.

definition: A connecting method of shooting and editing so that one action flows naturally between different shots.
example: Match the position and speed of the hand grabbing the doorknob and connect them with match action.

definition: An expression that a discontinuity stands out because action, position, or time suddenly differs between cuts.
example: The hand holding the glass differs from cut to cut, so the connection jumps; look at another take.

definition: Feedback that the pacing of a scene or edit runs longer than intended, reducing tension or interest.
example: The same explanation continues and the middle drags, so trim the redundant dialogue.

definition: A working expression for compressing the pacing by reducing unnecessary pauses or repetition in editing.
example: Please trim the silences between answers a bit and cut them together more tightly.
note: This entry means tightening the editing pace. Distinguish it from the usages of requesting a tighter framing in shooting or saying there is no schedule slack.

definition: A method of connecting a transition by carrying music, ambient sound, or dialogue across the preceding and following scenes.
example: Use the train sound heard first as a sound bridge to move to the next location.

definition: A track used temporarily instead of the final music to set the mood and timing of the edit.
example: Reference the mood of the temp music, but confirm the usage rights of the final track separately.

definition: Feedback recording revision requests for an edit and the like, together with timecode, subject, and desired result.
example: In the review notes, write the exact timecode and the corrected subtitle text.
note: This is the context of video post-production feedback. Rather than only recording taste, leave the subject and desired change specifically.

definition: The work of managing the relationship between people and work, such as recruiting, placement, evaluation, compensation, and organizational operation.
example: HR compiles the headcount plans by department.

definition: The organization responsible for HR systems and operations from an employee's hire to departure.
example: Check the effective date of the assignment with the HR team.

definition: The work of designing the workforce structure and HR systems such as evaluation, compensation, and job grades.
example: HR planning reviews the impact of the new job-grade system.

definition: The work of routinely executing systems such as HR information, assignments, certificates, and onboarding and offboarding.
example: The HR operations owner checks for missing onboarding documents.

definition: A role that collaborates with a specific business unit to solve workforce and organizational problems and connect HR systems.
example: Discuss the workforce impact of the reorganization with the business unit HRBP.

definition: Activities that manage an organization's workforce through recruiting, placement, evaluation, compensation, and so on.
example: Split HRM metrics into recruiting and retention areas.

definition: Activities that build employees' capabilities through training, career development, and so on.
example: The HRD owner prepares the new-leader training.

definition: A person who organizes hiring needs and runs candidate sourcing, screening, and onboarding.
example: Deliver the interview feedback to the recruiter.

definition: A role that finds and contacts target talent for hiring and builds the candidate pool.
example: The sourcer finds candidates with the relevant technical experience.

definition: The person in the hiring organization who leads the required competencies and selection decisions.
example: Define the scope of required experience with the hiring manager.

definition: The work area dealing with compensation systems such as pay, incentives, and benefits.
example: The C&B owner reviews the salary ranges and benefit costs.

definition: The organization responsible for improving organizational culture, such as ways of working, values, and communication experience.
example: Share the internal survey results with the organizational culture team.

definition: A person responsible for operating working conditions, labor-management relations, and labor-related systems.
example: Check the procedure for changing the work system with the labor relations officer.

definition: An organization name for the HR function centered on employee experience and organizational operation.
example: The People team reviews the onboarding adaptation process.

definition: The person responsible for overseeing the organization's HR strategy and major HR functions.
example: Report the annual workforce plan to the Head of HR.

definition: A system that manages HR data such as employee information, assignments, and attendance.
example: Check whether the department in the HRIS matches the assignment.

definition: The core data that serves as the basis for HR work, such as employee ID, affiliation, job grade, and hire date.
example: Reflect the changes in the HR master data before running payroll.

definition: An official measure announcing an employee's HR change such as hiring, promotion, or transfer.
example: Distinguish the effective date and the announcement date of the personnel order.

definition: Material that depicts the department composition and reporting relationships in a diagram.
example: Update the organization chart once the reorganization is complete.

definition: A document organizing a job's purpose, responsibilities, tasks, and required competencies.
example: Specify the scope of responsibility in the job description before hiring.

definition: A plan that sets the number of hires, jobs, timing, and budget according to business and organizational needs.
example: Reflect the new-business headcount in the quarterly hiring plan.

definition: A document in which a department states the reason for filling, the job, the number of people, and so on to request hiring approval.
example: State in the hiring requisition whether it is a backfill or an addition.

definition: The number of people belonging to an organization or the approved headcount size.
example: Align whether people on leave are included, then compare headcount.

definition: The number of people allocated or approved for an organization or job.
example: Check whether hiring is possible within the team's authorized headcount.

definition: The number of people actually placed as of a reference point.
example: Organize the gap between authorized and current headcount by department.

definition: The work of filling insufficient or vacant workforce.
example: Set the staffing-up timing considering the work of the departing employee.

definition: The work of increasing the previously set headcount size.
example: Request added headcount to operate the new store.

definition: Hiring to fill a vacancy created by departure, transfer, and so on.
example: Distinguish whether this hiring is an addition or a backfill.

definition: A recruitment notice made public so applicants can learn the job, qualifications, and process.
example: Write the actual responsibilities and the screening order in the job posting.

definition: A system that manages applicant information and hiring stages, interview records, and so on.
example: Check the candidates awaiting interviews in the ATS.

definition: A set of candidates managed with future hiring potential in mind.
example: Confirm consent to store the information and register them in the talent pool.

definition: A method of directly finding and contacting suitable candidates instead of waiting for applications to a posting.
example: For experienced-hire positions, also run direct sourcing.

definition: A hiring channel in which current employees introduce suitable candidates to the company.
example: Review referral candidates by the same evaluation standard.

definition: A selection stage that reviews career, competency, and application conditions through application documents.
example: Align the document screening criteria with the interviewers first.

definition: An interview method that prepares common questions and evaluation criteria to compare candidates.
example: Organize the evaluation scale per question for the structured interview.

definition: An interview that checks job-performance competency through actual experience and behavioral examples.
example: In the competency interview, ask about specific actions taken to resolve a conflict.

definition: A form for recording the evidence confirmed in the interview and the evaluation results.
example: In the interview evaluation form, write the confirmed examples rather than impressions.

definition: The process of verifying past work experience and so on, following the candidate's consent and proper procedures.
example: Set the reference check items to job-related content.

definition: The process of negotiating pay, job grade, and working conditions before joining.
example: In the offer negotiation, explain the fixed pay and variable pay separately.

definition: A document in which the company proposes employment conditions to a candidate.
example: Finally confirm the start date and compensation terms in the offer letter.

definition: The proportion of candidates who accepted the offer among those who received one.
example: Align the aggregation period, then compare the offer acceptance rate.

definition: The time elapsed between defined start and end points, such as from the hiring request to filling.
example: Unify the start point of time to fill as the approval date.

definition: The amount of cost spent on hiring activities aggregated by a defined scope and standard, or the cost per person.
example: Include external fees and advertising costs in the cost per hire.

definition: The process of helping new members adapt to the work, organization, and systems.
example: Include a guide to system access in the onboarding schedule.

definition: The process of handover, settlement, and access revocation in line with departure or contract end.
example: Check account revocation with the offboarding checklist.
